prompts: Who are the users, and how many? Peak versus average traffic?
What data, how much, how sensitive? Any compliance (PCI, HIPAA, residency)?
Budget, timeline, and the team's skills. What does success look like?
One box per tier, request path left to right.
Say what each box does in one sentence.
Where is the first bottleneck? Stateless tiers scale out; state moves to managed stores.
Caching (CloudFront, ElastiCache), queues to absorb spikes, read replicas.
Multi-AZ everywhere it matters. What happens when each box dies?
Retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, health checks, a DR tier tied to RPO and RTO.
Private subnets, least-privilege roles, encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS).
WAF at the edge, CloudTrail for audit, secrets in Secrets Manager.
What drives the bill? Right-size, Savings Plans for baseline, Spot or serverless for spikes.
Lifecycle rules for storage; state a rough cost direction, not a fake exact number.
"I chose X over Y because Z; I would revisit if W."
Close with the next step: a proof of concept or a Well-Architected review.

designs.title: 3-tier web app for a retailer with Black Friday spikes
designs.prompt: A retailer's site slows down and sometimes fails on peak days like Black Friday. Design an AWS architecture that stays fast and up.
clarifying: How big is the spike versus a normal day, and is the date known in advance?
Is the slowness in the web tier, the database, or checkout?
Global or US-only users? Any PCI scope for payments?

non_functional: Page loads fast for users across the country

components.name: CloudFront + WAF
components.role: Caches images and pages at the edge, blocks bots

components.name: Aurora Multi-AZ + read replicas
components.role: Orders and catalog; replicas serve reads

components.name: SQS
components.role: Buffers order processing so checkout accepts orders even when downstream is slow

flow: User resolves the domain in Route 53 and hits CloudFront; cached images and pages return from the edge.
Cache misses go to the ALB, then to app servers in an Auto Scaling group across 2 AZs.
App servers read sessions and hot catalog data from ElastiCache, the rest from Aurora read replicas.
Checkout writes the order to Aurora and puts fulfillment work on SQS for workers to process.
scale: Scheduled scaling to pre-warm before the known peak, plus target tracking on request count
Cache aggressively at CloudFront and ElastiCache so the database sees a fraction of traffic
Queue order fulfillment so spikes do not hit downstream systems directly
security: WAF rate limits and bot control at CloudFront
App and database in private subnets
Payment data kept out of scope via a tokenizing payment provider
cost: Savings Plans for the baseline fleet, On-Demand or Spot for the peak
Scale back down after the event
designs.tradeoff: Pre-warming with scheduled scaling costs money before the peak, but reactive scaling alone can lag a sudden spike. For a known date I pay for headroom; I would revisit if the spike were unpredictable.

failure_modes.mitigation: ALB routes to healthy AZs; Aurora fails over to its standby
Cache hits plus read replicas; protect writes
SQS buffers orders; dead-letter queue catches poison messages

followups: How would you test this before Black Friday?
What if traffic is 10x what they predicted?
How do you keep sessions if an instance dies?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Users"] --> R53["Route 53"] --> CF["CloudFront + WAF"]
  CF --> S3["S3 assets"]
  CF --> ALB["ALB"] --> ASG["App servers, ASG over 2 AZs"]
  ASG --> EC["ElastiCache"]
  ASG --> AUR["Aurora Multi-AZ + replicas"]
  ASG --> Q["SQS orders"] --> W["Fulfillment workers"]

designs.title: Migrate an on-prem ERP and financial system to AWS
designs.prompt: A mid-size company runs its ERP and financial reporting on premises. Their data center lease ends in a year. Plan the move to AWS.
clarifying: Which workloads, how many, and how coupled are they?
Audit and compliance rules on financial data? Allowed downtime at cutover?
Is the ERP vendor offering a SaaS version?

functional: Every ERP workload moved or retired
Financial reports reconcile before and after

components.name: Control Tower
components.role: Multi-account landing zone with guardrails and central logging

components.name: Application Migration Service
components.role: Rehost servers that stay as they are

components.name: DMS + Schema Conversion
components.role: Database migration with change data capture

flow: Discover: inventory every workload and map dependencies.
Decide a 7 R per workload: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, refactor.
Build the landing zone with Control Tower; connect on-prem with VPN, then Direct Connect.
Replicate databases with DMS change data capture; run parallel reconciliation reports.
Cut over in waves, lowest risk first; keep rollback until finance signs off.
scale: Migrate in waves so the team learns on low-risk workloads first
Automate repeatable steps for later waves
security: Separate accounts for prod, non-prod, logging, security
KMS encryption, CloudTrail organization trail, least-privilege roles
cost: Retire unused workloads first; they are pure savings
Right-size after a few weeks of real usage, then commit to Savings Plans
designs.tradeoff: Rehost gets out of the data center fastest; replatform or repurchase saves more long term. I would rehost what blocks the exit date and modernize the rest after the move.

failure_modes.failure: Data drift between source and target
failure_modes.mitigation: DMS change data capture plus automated reconciliation reports, like the field-level checks in S1
Dependency mapping up front, wave planning, rollback plan
Rehearse the cutover; define go and no-go criteria

followups: Which 7 R would you pick for the ERP itself, and why?
How do you prove the books still balance?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  ON["On-prem ERP + DB"] -- "VPN / Direct Connect" --> LZ["Landing zone, Control Tower"]
  ON --> MGN["Application Migration Service"] --> EC2["Rehosted servers"]
  ON --> DMS["DMS with CDC"] --> RDS["RDS / Aurora"]
  RDS --> REC["Reconciliation reports, S3 + Athena"]
  LZ --> EC2
  LZ --> RDS

designs.title: Serverless document processing pipeline
designs.prompt: An insurance company receives thousands of claim documents a day as PDFs. Extract the data, summarize each claim, and route uncertain ones to a person.
clarifying: Volume per day and peak per hour? Document types and quality?
How fast must a claim be processed? What accuracy is acceptable?

non_functional: Pay per document, not per idle server

components.name: A2I or a task-token review queue
components.role: Human review below the confidence threshold

flow: A document lands in S3; EventBridge starts a Step Functions execution.
Textract extracts fields; Bedrock summarizes and scores confidence.
Above the threshold, results go straight to DynamoDB.
Below it, the workflow pauses for a human reviewer, then writes the corrected result.
scale: Every step is serverless and scales with load
Use Textract asynchronous APIs for multi-page documents
Queue in front of Bedrock calls if model quotas are the limit
security: S3 encryption with KMS, block public access
Macie to find PII; Bedrock Guardrails to redact PII in summaries
cost: Pay per document and per token; no idle servers
designs.tradeoff: A lower confidence threshold means fewer human reviews and lower cost, but more risk of a wrong claim slipping through. Start conservative and lower it as reviewers stop correcting results, as I did in S1.

failure_modes.mitigation: Step Functions retries with backoff; request quota increases ahead of time
Route to human review instead of guessing
Idempotency key per document in DynamoDB

followups: How do you measure extraction accuracy?
How do you keep PII out of model logs?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  UP["Upload"] --> S3["S3"] --> EB["EventBridge"] --> SF["Step Functions"]
  SF --> TX["Textract"]
  SF --> BR["Bedrock summary + confidence"]
  BR -- "high" --> DDB["DynamoDB results"]
  BR -- "low" --> HR["Human review"] --> DDB

designs.title: GenAI chatbot over company docs (RAG)
designs.prompt: A company wants an internal assistant that answers employee questions from its policies and wikis, with sources. Design it on AWS.
clarifying: How many documents, where do they live, how often do they change?
Who may see which documents? Any data that must never reach the model?
How will we know answers are good enough to launch?

non_functional: Low hallucination rate on an evaluation set

components.name: Bedrock model + Guardrails
components.role: Generates grounded answers; filters PII and off-topic requests

flow: Documents in S3 sync into the Knowledge Base, which chunks and embeds them into the vector store.
An employee signs in and asks a question through API Gateway and Lambda.
The Knowledge Base retrieves the most relevant chunks, filtered by the user's permissions.
The model answers from those chunks with citations; Guardrails check input and output.
scale: Serverless API and vector store scale with use
Use a smaller model where evaluation shows it is good enough
security: Metadata filters so users only retrieve documents they may read
Guardrails for PII and denied topics
Customer data is not used to train the base models
cost: Cost per question is mostly tokens: keep retrieved context tight
Pick the smallest model that passes the evaluation set
designs.tradeoff: A larger model answers better but costs more per question. I would build an evaluation set first, try the smallest model, and only move up when it fails, the same reasoning as my ModelScope study.

failure_modes.mitigation: Require citations; grounding checks; say "I don't know" when retrieval is weak
Scheduled or event-driven sync from S3

failure_modes.failure: User sees a document they should not
failure_modes.mitigation: Permission metadata filters at retrieval time, tested before launch

followups: How do you evaluate answer quality before launch?
How do you handle a question that needs live data from a system?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DOC["S3 docs"] --> KB["Bedrock Knowledge Base"] --> VS["Vector store"]
  EMP["Employee"] --> AUTH["Cognito / Identity Center"] --> API["API Gateway + Lambda"]
  API --> KB
  API --> LLM["Bedrock model + Guardrails"]
  VS --> LLM

designs.title: Real-time clickstream analytics
designs.prompt: A media company wants to see what users click in near real time and analyze history for trends. Design the pipeline.
clarifying: Events per second at peak? How fresh must dashboards be: seconds or minutes?
How long to keep raw history?
Who queries it and how often?

functional: Collect click events from web and apps

components.name: Kinesis Data Streams
components.role: Ingests events, ordered per shard, replayable

components.name: Data Firehose
components.role: Batches and writes events to S3 in Parquet

flow: Apps send events to Kinesis Data Streams.
A real-time consumer updates live metrics; Firehose batches the same stream into S3 as Parquet.
Glue catalogs the data; Athena queries it; QuickSight shows dashboards.
scale: Add shards or use on-demand capacity mode
Partition S3 by date and use columnar Parquet so Athena scans less
security: Encrypt streams and buckets with KMS
Lake Formation for column-level access to user data
cost: Athena charges per data scanned: partitions and Parquet cut it
Lifecycle raw data to cheaper tiers
designs.tradeoff: Firehose buffering makes data land in S3 within minutes, not seconds. That is fine for history; true real-time metrics come from a stream consumer instead.

failure_modes.failure: Hot shard from one popular key
failure_modes.mitigation: Better partition key or random suffix
Validate at ingest; send bad records to an error prefix

followups: How do you handle late-arriving events?
What would you change at 10x volume?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP["Web and apps"] --> KDS["Kinesis Data Streams"]
  KDS --> RT["Real-time consumer"] --> DASH["Live metrics"]
  KDS --> FH["Data Firehose"] --> S3["S3 Parquet lake"]
  S3 --> GL["Glue Catalog"] --> ATH["Athena"] --> QS["QuickSight"]

designs.title: Multi-region DR for a payments app
designs.prompt: A payments company runs in one Region. Regulators and customers want it to survive a full Region outage. Design the DR approach.
clarifying: What RPO and RTO does the business need, in minutes?
Which flows must survive: payments only, or reporting too?
Any data residency rules that limit which Regions?

functional: Fail over to a second Region

components.name: Route 53 failover routing + health checks
components.role: Moves traffic to the healthy Region

components.name: Aurora Global Database
components.role: Cross-Region replication with low lag; promote the secondary on failover

components.name: DynamoDB global tables
components.role: Multi-Region idempotency keys and session data

components.name: Application stack in both Regions
components.role: Warm standby or active/active, built with IaC

flow: Pick the DR tier from RPO and RTO: payments usually need warm standby or active/active.
Primary Region serves traffic; Aurora Global Database replicates to the secondary.
Health checks fail, Route 53 shifts traffic, the secondary Aurora cluster is promoted.
Idempotency keys stop a retried payment from charging twice.
scale: Warm standby runs small and scales up on failover
Active/active doubles capacity cost but removes the scale-up step
security: Same IAM and guardrails deployed by IaC in both
cost: Each tier up the DR ladder costs more: match it to the business RPO and RTO, not to fear
designs.tradeoff: Active/active gives near-zero RTO but makes writes harder (conflicts, double processing). For payments I would start with warm standby plus idempotency and move to active/active only if the RTO demands it.

failure_modes.mitigation: Scheduled game days that actually fail over
Monitor lag against RPO; reconcile after failover

failure_modes.failure: Split brain: both Regions accept writes
failure_modes.mitigation: Single writer with explicit promotion, or conflict-safe idempotent design

followups: What RPO and RTO would you propose, and how do you prove them?
What does this cost compared with today?
designs.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Clients"] --> R53["Route 53 failover"]
  R53 --> P["Primary Region app"]
  R53 -. "on failure" .-> S["Secondary Region app"]
  P --> AP["Aurora primary"]
  S --> AS["Aurora secondary"]
  AP -- "Global Database replication" --> AS
  P --> DG["DynamoDB global table"]
  S --> DG
